title: Identification of optimal BAL sample processing strategy through comparative assessment of qPCR BAL results
abstract: Microbial communities in the lung are poorly defined and play an unknown role in mediating disease. Next generation sequencing techniques unveiled novel insights into various human microbiomes; however, current sample processing methods limit the application of this powerful tool in the study of lung microbiomes. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL), a common diagnostic tool used to sample the lower respiratory tract, yields abundant human DNA that leads to poor microbial genome assembly (i.e., metagenomes). To address these challenges, we aim to investigate the impact of different sample processing methods on microbial and human DNA yield, and thereby to identify optimal strategies to sequence lung metagenomes. Currently, a stepwise optimization strategy is being implemented to process BAL samples through different combinations of treatments to reduce human DNA carryover while maintaining microbial DNA concentrations. Further work in this ongoing project aims to use quantitative methods to determine the yield of human and microbial DNA. We aim on quantifying the absolute abundance of bacterial/human DNA in each sample through quantitative PCR (qPCR) and assessing the bias between sample processing methods by assessing sample metagenomes through 16S ribosomal RNA gene sequencing and performing beta-diversity analysis. The results of qPCR quantification and bias analysis through 16S will inform which method of BAL fluid preparation is most suitable for subsequent lung microbiome analysis using whole genome shotgun metagenomic sequencing, thus providing a tool for future research on lower respiratory tract infections and lung microbial ecology. This research will ultimately aid the development of microbiome-targeted therapeutics for lung diseases such as pneumonia or cystic fibrosis.
